summary:
ARGUS bridges the gap between raw space data and everyday people. NASA's SPHEREx telescope maps the entire sky in 102 infrared colors, but this incredible data is locked inside complex FITS files that require specialized software to open. We built a zero-install, browser-based pipeline that turns any laptop into a mission-control terminal.

Users can target any coordinate or pick from five pre-cached targets to view real SPHEREx time-series images. We built Blink and Difference imaging modes, allowing anyone to spot candidate moving objects against static stars.

We didn't just build a photo viewer; we built a scientific instrument. Our backend uses wavelength matching (comparing frames within 0.2 µm) to prevent fake brightness changes. We validated our pipeline on Barnard's Star, honestly reporting our measured shift (17.58 px) vs predicted catalog motion (9.33 px). ARGUS democratizes citizen science, empowering students and astronomers to explore the cosmos using real NASA data.
details:
What does it do?
ARGUS is a public-facing web tool that makes raw NASA SPHEREx telescope data accessible to anyone. Users can input sky coordinates or select from 5 pre-cached targets to view time-series infrared images of the sky directly in a browser.

How does it work?
We built a full-stack scientific pipeline. Our Python backend (FastAPI) connects directly to the NASA/IPAC IRSA archive using the Table Access Protocol (TAP). It downloads raw FITS image cutouts in parallel, reads the true wavelengths from the file headers, aligns the frames, and converts them into web-ready PNGs. The frontend (Vite, Three.js) provides an interactive 3D globe and a mission-control HUD.

What benefits does it have? (Impact)
Historically, finding moving objects like asteroids required downloading massive files and using specialized software. ARGUS democratizes citizen science. It turns any laptop into a scientific terminal, allowing students, educators, and amateur astronomers to spot moving objects by eye with zero installation.

How is your project creative?
We built a highly visual, sci-fi-inspired UI that includes Play, Blink, and Difference imaging modes. Difference mode cancels out static stars entirely, leaving only the moving candidate glowing.

What factors did your team consider? (Validity & Honesty)
We prioritized radical scientific honesty.

  1. Wavelength Matching: If you compare a red-filter image to a blue-filter image, a star looks brighter, but it's a fake change. Our backend only compares frames within 0.2 micrometers of each other.
  2. Validation Box: We don't fake discoveries. We built a live validation box that reports our actual mathematical findings. For Barnard's Star, the measured shift was 17.58 px against a predicted 9.33 px. We show this size gap transparently.
  3. Raw Data: We kept the messy detector edge artifacts (like the diagonal line on Epsilon Indi B) visible to prove we aren't photoshopping the data.

Tools & Technologies Used:
Python, FastAPI, Astropy, PyVO, Vite, Vanilla JS, Three.js, CSS. AI was used as a co-pilot for boilerplate code, while all scientific logic and UI design were human-directed.
